title: Hooked
author: Nir Eyal
thesisParagraph: Products become habitual when they repeatedly connect a user's felt problem to a simple action, an unpredictable reward, and a small investment that makes returning more likely. Habit design is strongest when it is measured, ethically bounded, and tied to a real user need rather than mere attention capture.

signatureMoves: uses triggers, traction, distraction, investment, and pacts as named mechanisms
moves quickly from user psychology to product or attention design
asks what internal trigger is being relieved before blaming the tool
keeps diagrams and acronyms close to real behavior loops
opens concepts with familiar consumer-technology scenarios before naming the behavioral mechanism
avoidMoves: Avoid "The point is" as a paragraph hinge.
Avoid "the question is" as a setup crutch.
Avoid triadic abstract-noun lists such as clarity, courage, and resilience.
Do not blame technology before naming the internal trigger.
Do not make behavior design sound like manipulation without mechanism.
does not linger in abstract theory after introducing a behavioral concept
does not write in a literary or memoir-heavy register

voiceSpecimens: A product becomes habit when the itch and the trigger learn each other's address.
The loop works only after the user invests a little of themselves.
teachingArc: The opening establishes why habits matter commercially and how to tell whether a product belongs in the Habit Zone. The middle four stages teach the Hook Model in order: trigger, action, variable reward, and investment. The ending adds ethical screening, demonstrates the full loop through YouVersion, and turns the framework into a testing and opportunity-finding process.
forbiddenMoves: Do not turn Eyal into generic focus advice.
Do not skip the loop structure when explaining habit or distraction.
